planting.note: Plant divisions in early fall or spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Humpback Whale is one of the largest hostas bred by the late Mildred Seaver and needs a generous footprint of 6 feet or more in every direction to reach its full mounded form.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, siting it where its eventual bulk will not crowd neighboring perennials. Humpback Whale forms a massive dome of heavily corrugated, blue-green leaves that are at their bluest in spring before fading toward green as summer heat arrives, with scapes of white flowers rising well above the foliage in early summer. Give it several seasons of consistent moisture and rich soil to bulk up, since giant Hosta sieboldiana-type cultivars like this one are slow to show their full size. It works best as a solitary specimen or anchor plant rather than in a tightly spaced mass planting.

common_name: Allan P. McConnell Hosta (Small Green and White Groundcover Hosta)

planting.note: Plant in spring or early fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to part sun; this older Mildred Seaver introduction spreads steadily by underground shoots as well as division, making it one of the better true groundcover hostas.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in part sun to partial shade; Allan P. McConnell tolerates more direct sun than most hostas and multiplies quickly both by division and by spreading underground shoots, making it a reliable small-scale groundcover rather than a single-clump specimen. Rounded, heart-shaped, medium green leaves edged in a narrow band of clean white form a tidy, fast-filling mound, topped by short spikes of dark purple flowers in midsummer. Because it spreads on its own, give it room to knit together into a continuous patch rather than spacing it as widely as a clumping hosta, and divide only when you want to start new drifts elsewhere in the garden.

common_name: Queen of the Seas Hosta (Large Blue Piecrust-Margined Hosta)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; this large Mildred Seaver introduction takes a few seasons to show its signature piecrust-edged leaves at full size.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Queen of the Seas forms a fountain-shaped mound of thick, pointed, blue-green leaves whose ruffled, piecrust-like margins catch the light and set it apart from smoother-leaved blue hostas. The heavy leaf substance gives it noticeably better slug resistance than thin-leaved cultivars, and the fountain habit makes it a good textural contrast next to mounded or gold-leaved hostas nearby. Pale lavender flowers appear on scapes held above the foliage in summer. Allow it room to reach its full width before crowding in companion plants, since the arching leaves spread outward well beyond the base of the clump.

common_name: Blue Flame Hosta (Powder-Blue Hosta with Cream Margin)

planting.note: Plant in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Blue Flame is a creamy-edged sport of 'Fragrant Blue' named and introduced by Naylor Creek Nursery, forming a tidy medium-sized mound.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Blue Flame carries powdery, pale blue leaves rimmed in an irregular cream margin that shifts toward yellow with celadon streaking as the season progresses, giving the clump a two-toned, almost flickering look. Lightly fragrant lavender flowers rise on scapes above the foliage in midsummer, a trait inherited from its 'Fragrant Blue' parent. Keep the soil consistently moist through summer to preserve the blue cast of the leaves, since drought stress and intense sun can push the color toward flat green. Its compact medium size suits borders and mixed shade plantings where larger blue hostas would overwhelm the space.

common_name: Royal Mouse Ears Hosta (Miniature Sport of Blue Mouse Ears)

planting.note: Plant divisions in early fall or spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Royal Mouse Ears is a slow-growing miniature sport of 'Blue Mouse Ears' registered by E. & J. Deckert, best suited to rock gardens, troughs, and container culture.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Royal Mouse Ears is a miniature sport of the popular 'Blue Mouse Ears,' sharing its parent's thick, rounded, deeply cupped leaves but originally showing cream streaking that has faded to a mostly solid blue-green with age in many garden clumps. Bell-shaped, pale lavender, lightly striped flowers appear in early summer on short scapes that barely clear the foliage. Growth is notably slow even by mouse-ear standards, so resist dividing a young clump and instead let it fill its space over several seasons. The glaucous, waxy leaf surface gives it good resistance to slug damage compared with thinner-leaved miniatures, making it a dependable choice for small shaded nooks.

common_name: Half and Half Hosta (Tricolor White-Centered Hosta)

planting.note: Plant in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Half and Half, a sport of 'Lakeside Cupcake' discovered and registered by Naylor Creek Nursery, shows its strongest white-and-blue-green contrast in cooler, protected shade.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Half and Half opens each spring with a nearly pure white center bordered by a thin band of light green and an outer margin of strongly corrugated blue-green, giving the clump a layered, three-color effect that is unusual even among variegated hostas. The thick, heavily textured leaves offer better-than-average slug resistance, and lavender flowers appear on scapes above the foliage in summer. Because the white center can scorch in strong or prolonged sun, keep this cultivar in reliably shaded, evenly moist sites rather than the brighter edge conditions some green-centered hostas tolerate. Its compact size makes it well suited to borders and smaller shaded beds.

common_name: Funky Monkey Hosta (Chartreuse Hosta with Dark Petioles)

planting.note: Plant in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Funky Monkey, registered through the American Hosta Society, colors best with a little morning light to bring out its chartreuse and gold tones.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with a little morning light; Funky Monkey emerges bright chartreuse with striking dark purple-black petioles that carry color up into the leaf veins, a combination that makes it stand out even before the unusual leaf-color shifts of midsummer appear. As the season progresses, the leaf centers on many shoots turn deeper gold while the margins hold a lustrous green, producing irregular, ever-changing variegation patterns unlike typical edge- or center-variegated hostas. The shiny, moderately rippled leaves have good substance, and pale lavender flowers bloom from late summer into fall, later than most hostas. Give it room to spread into a large mound, since it is one of the bigger cultivars in its color class, and note that the sport 'Monkey Business' was later bred from it by Naylor Creek Nursery.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Hosta Selection for Shade
